Kaylub Giamanco was on his lunch break when he heard gunshots at his daughter’s school. He didn’t hesitate for a second, but rushed to the school with his own weapon, found the shooter, and killed him. Then he called his mother, and she shared what he told her after his heroic action.
Of course, the experience was incredibly traumatic for Giamanco, not only because he had to kill someone at point-blank range, while unsure if his girls were okay, but because he is wrongly blaming himself for not getting to the shooter before the crazed teenager killed three children and a teacher. Giamanco is pictured on the left below, while the shooter, Griffin J. John, is on the right.
Three little boys and a 25-year-old teacher are dead. An armed dad stopped it from being worse. * Griffin J. John II, 16, walked to Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, Oregon. * He threw a shotgun over the fence and climbed in. * He shot out the glass on the locked doors. * He went straight into the special-needs classroom, where he was a former student there. - Killed: boys ages 5, 8 and 11, including Rhoam Summer, 5. - Killed: teacher Megan Lambert, 25. Her family says she "always fought for the underdog and those with special needs." -A 7-year-old in a wheelchair was shot in the face. -An aide, 54, was also wounded. - He still had 44 rounds on him. - Officials say his mother bought the shotgun around his birthday in August. - No school resource officer was there. That one officer covers 6 or 7 schools. - A teacher threw her phone at him and fought him for the gun. - Then dad Kaylub Giamanco, 36, ran in with his legally carried pistol and shot him dead. A good guy with a gun saved lives. Again.
— Kentucky Girl (@Kentuckygirl1) October 17, 2026
Kenda Freeman, Giamanco’s mother, shared the story through tears in a clip that CBS News Sacramento posted. Freeman is from California, but her son has been living in Oregon and raising a family there for years. His daughters attend Silver Rail Elementary School, where John murdered four people and injured two others, including a wheelchair-bound kid.
MOTHER OF HERO SPEAKS OUT 🙏🏼 Kaylub Giamanco’s mom just described the phone call she got moments after her son stopped the school shooter in Bend, Oregon. “He said, Mom, I just shot and kiIIed somebody.” She asked him to tell her about it. “A man went into my daughter’s school and shot kids. And I looked at him point blank and I shot and kiIIed him, Mom.” She told him he saved a lot of lives. His answer: “Mom, I couldn’t save them all.” He was driving home from lunch when he heard the shots. He pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun, and followed the gunman back into the school. He army-crawled through a window the shooter had already blasted out and ended the attack. Three kids and a teacher were already gone. His own daughters were safe. Now he’s struggling with the ones he couldn’t reach and asking himself what he could have done differently. This is what happens when a good man with a gun runs toward the sound of gunfire instead of waiting for someone else to show up. THAT is what stopped more of them from dying. Kaylub Giamanco is a hero.
— TONY™ (@TONYxTWO) October 17, 2026
Giamanco called up his mother right after the shooting. “He said, ‘Mom, I just shot and killed somebody.’ I said, ‘Kaylub, tell me about it.’ And he said, ‘A man went into my daughters’ school and, um... shot kids.’ And he said, ‘and I looked at him point-blank, and I shot and killed him, Mom.’ I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, ‘Mom, I couldn't save them all.’”
People around the nation, including President Donald Trump, are praising Giamanco for ensuring the massacre was not even worse. He and a teacher who tackled John put their own lives on the line to save as many kids as possible. But while no one could possibly have expected Giamanco to do more, he is still devastated that other families had to bring their kids home in coffins.

Freeman explained, teary-eyed, “Kaylub has a genuine heart, he loves his community. Kaylub knew something was not right. So he pulled up onto the grass, grabbed his gun and basically stalked the gunman back into the school. And he crawled through a window that the gunman had shot out. He army-crawled through the window. It's tough, because I'm... while I'm thankful that my babies are okay, there are babies that are not. And that's, um, that's hard to swallow, 'cause my heart goes out to those families that didn't get to bring their babies home.”
Giamanco is also “having a hard time with it. Again, you know, the idea of not being able to save them all, right? So when he closes his eyes and the things that he thinks about, what could I have done differently? How could I have done it better?” Freeman added.
One thing is certain — without Giamanco’s courage, even more teachers and children would have died.

sources.news_title: 'Not Seeking Recognition': Bend Father Honored for Stopping School Shooter
sources.text:
The Briefing
- A 16-year-old gunman forced entry into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on October 15, 2026, killing three boys and a 25-year-old teacher inside a special needs classroom before being shot and killed by a community member.
- The bystander, identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco, 36, is a lifelong Bend resident who had two daughters enrolled at the school and carried a legally permitted handgun.
- Among the dead is 5-year-old Rhoam Summer, identified by authorities as the youngest child to die in a U.S. school shooting since the 1960s.
A 36-year-old man driving near Silver Rail Elementary School made a decision on Thursday that authorities say cut short a massacre in progress. Kaylub Giamanco, a lifelong Bend resident whose two daughters attend the school, spotted an armed teenager entering the building, retrieved his legally permitted handgun, and ran through the same shattered doors the shooter had just forced open — emerging minutes later after killing the attacker inside.
A Peaceful Community Shattered in Minutes
The attack began at approximately 12:59 p.m. local time on October 15 at Silver Rail Elementary, a kindergarten-through-fifth-grade campus serving roughly 459 students in Bend, a central Oregon city of around 100,000 people situated about 175 miles southeast of Portland. The first emergency calls reported a shot fired into a vehicle in the parking lot. Within seconds, additional 911 calls placed from inside the building told a far grimmer story.
When officers finished their sweep of the building, four people were dead: three boys ages 5, 8, and 11, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert. Two additional victims — a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old educational assistant — were transported to St. Charles Medical Center with critical injuries. Among the youngest killed was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer, whom authorities have noted is the youngest child to die in a U.S. school shooting since the 1960s.
Who Was the Shooter?
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a local resident who had previously attended Silver Rail as a special needs student and was no longer enrolled in the district at the time of the attack. He forced entry by firing repeatedly at locked glass doors with a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun — a weapon his mother had reportedly purchased, according to multiple officials who spoke with NBC News.
Superintendent Steven Cook of Bend-La Pine Schools confirmed that every victim who was shot had been inside a mixed-age special education classroom, a detail that deepened the horror facing investigators still working to establish a motive.
The Moment a Father Chose to Run Toward the Danger
Giamanco was driving near the school when the sound of gunfire and the sight of an armed figure entering the building made the situation unmistakable. He retrieved his handgun and ran inside, holding a valid concealed carry permit, his family confirmed through ABC News.
Inside, he found the suspect already engaged in a confrontation with a teacher who was fighting to take the shotgun away. After assessing the threat, Giamanco fired and ended the attack. Police arriving moments later found the scene already contained. Chief Krantz credited Giamanco's swift action as the decisive intervention that prevented additional casualties.
Praise From the White House to the Governor's Office
The response from elected officials was swift and, in its political overtones, predictably divided — though the praise for Giamanco himself crossed party lines. President Donald Trump described the father as a "great hero" and stated, "Thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," remarks delivered to reporters at the White House on Friday that immediately amplified the national debate over armed civilians and school safety.
Oregon's Democratic Governor Tina Kotek took a more measured but equally supportive tone, publicly thanking Giamanco for heroically intervening to stop further loss of life. She ordered flags across the state lowered to half-staff and attended a vigil that evening in Bend's Drake Park, where thousands of community members gathered alongside Mayor Melanie Kebler to grieve together.
The Teacher Who Fought Back First
Authorities were also careful to acknowledge the bravery of the unnamed teacher who physically confronted the gunman before Giamanco arrived. According to police accounts confirmed by local authorities, she threw her cellphone at the attacker and then tackled him in an attempt to strip the shotgun from his hands — an act of courage that police said almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed. She was not injured in the confrontation.
Separately, Becky Drury, a 54-year-old educational assistant in the special education department, was struck by gunfire and transported to St. Charles Medical Center, where she was treated for serious but non-life-threatening injuries, her family confirmed.
Megan Lambert: A Teacher Who Lived Her Dream
Megan Lambert, 25, was a Bend native and 2023 Boise State University graduate who had long dreamed of teaching in her hometown district. Her family, in a statement read at the Friday press conference, said Silver Rail was her first full-time teaching position and her "dream job." She had previously substituted at the school while completing her education. A volunteer volleyball coach who once turned down her coaching stipend so families in financial need could afford their children's participation, Lambert was remembered by colleagues as someone who consistently championed students with special needs.
A Hero Who Shuns the Spotlight
Despite the outpouring of recognition, Giamanco has declined all public attention. A statement released by his family said he is "not seeking recognition" and instead wants to direct gratitude toward first responders, school personnel, and the broader community. His family confirmed his identity and said he will not be granting interviews. Those close to him say he carries deep regret for the lives he could not reach in time.
The makeshift memorial that grew outside Silver Rail's entrance through the weekend — flowers, stuffed animals, handwritten notes from children — told the fuller story: of a community's grief, of impossible choices made under fire, and of a town where one man's instinct to protect the children inside a school will be impossible to forget.

sources.news_title: School shooting’s youngest victim, the killer, and the hero dad who took him down
Oregon school shooting: Gunman, 16 identified as Griffin J. John II; mother had bought weapon
Teen shooter who killed 4 at Oregon elementary school was a former student, police say – WTOP News
sources.text:
BEND, Ore. (AP) — A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
City of Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher’s actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
John was once a special needs student at Silver Rail Elementary, authorities said, and he attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
Investigators are trying to determine how the shooter obtained the pump-action shotgun, Krantz added.
A law enforcement official briefed on the shooting told The Associated Press it was bought by his mother. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
“I miss my boy,” Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun and didn’t comment further when The Associated Press and other outlets knocked on her apartment door later.
In a 2020 interview with the local news station KTVZ, Nickerson identified the boy, then 10, as a participant in a special needs program run by the school district. It was called NEST, for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust, and aimed at helping students experiencing intensive behavioral and social skill challenges. Nickerson said he struggled trying to learn from home during the pandemic.
Shooter killed minutes after first 911 call
The first 911 call came from the driver of a red pickup truck early Thursday afternoon who saw the boy throw his gun over a fence outside the school and then climb over it, Krantz said. The driver yelled at the boy, who fired at him, striking the truck three times. The driver was not injured.
A second driver, Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old man whose children attend Silver Rail, saw John shooting at the truck and heading toward the school, where he shot through locked doors to get inside. Giamanco pulled into the parking lot, grabbed his .40-caliber pistol and followed the attacker inside. He saw John wrestling with the teacher and shot him several times.
Three children — ages 5, 8 and 11 — and teacher Megan Lambert, 25, were killed, police said. A 7-year-old child who was injured received lifesaving care at the scene and is now hospitalized, as is 54-year-old teacher Becky Drury, who her family said was shot in the arm and hand and was recovering from surgery.
There were no other children in the classroom, authorities said.
The youngest victim, Rhoam Summer, was a fearless climber and a fast runner who loved reading, his aunt Swan Sheridan said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” she said.
Man who stopped the shooter a father of 2 at the school
In a statement read to reporters Friday, Giamanco’s mother, Kenda Freeman, identified him as the person who shot the gunman. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said.
She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time.”
Silver Rail Elementary has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 that has become a tourism and outdoor recreation hub in central Oregon.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the man who stopped the gunman, calling him a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.”
___
This story has been updated to correct the name of the teacher killed Thursday. She is Megan Lambert, not Meghan Lambert as police originally reported.
___
Associated Press reporters Alanna Durkin Richer, Eric Tucker and Ben Finley in Washington; Jamie Stengle in Dallas; Ed White in Detroit; Philip Marcelo in New York; and John Seewer in Toledo, Ohio, contributed.

sources.text:
Kaylub Giamanco was driving home for lunch on Thursday when he heard gunfire coming from Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where his two daughters are students. Moments later, the 36-year-old carpenter followed a teenage gunman into the school and shot him dead, ending a rampage that left four people dead, including three young children.
The attacker, identified by police as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, was a former student at the school who had attended special education classes. Armed with a 12-gauge Maverick 88 pump-action shotgun purchased by his mother, he shot his way through locked school doors and opened fire in a special education classroom, killing a teacher and three children aged 5, 8 and 11. A 7-year-old student and another teacher, 54, were also wounded.
At a news conference Friday, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz revealed that another teacher had attempted to stop the gunman before Giamanco intervened. The teacher threw her cellphone at the attacker, tackled him and struggled to take away his weapon. Police said she survived the confrontation without being injured.
"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said, praising her actions as heroic.
Investigators said the first confrontation occurred outside the school, when the teenage gunman threw his shotgun over a fence and climbed onto the school grounds. A driver in a red pickup truck shouted at him, prompting the attacker to open fire on the vehicle, striking it three times. The driver escaped unharmed and called 911.
Giamanco, who was passing nearby, witnessed the teenager shooting at the vehicle and heading toward the school. He pulled into the parking lot, took his .40-caliber pistol and pursued the attacker inside. There, he encountered the gunman struggling with the teacher and fired several shots, killing him.
Police said the attack unfolded within minutes. Investigators estimated that the teenager fired as many as 15 shotgun rounds and still had approximately 44 rounds of ammunition when he was killed.
'He doesn't feel like a hero'
Giamanco's brother, Kyle, told NBC News that despite being credited with preventing further bloodshed, his brother does not see himself as a hero. Instead, he is struggling with guilt over the lives he was unable to save. He has declined interview requests while he processes what happened.
Their mother, Kenda Freeman, told the New York Post that she was immensely proud of her son's quick thinking and courage. "He is absolutely a hero," she said, adding that he was going through an extremely difficult time.
Freeman also read a statement on behalf of the family, saying Giamanco was not seeking public recognition and wanted instead to thank first responders, school employees and members of the community for their support. His family, including his two daughters, requested privacy.
According to the New York Post, Giamanco had previously practiced shooting with U.S. military veterans who served in Iraq. In a September 2018 Facebook post, he described participating in shooting exercises with a group of former soldiers, thanking them for sharing their experience and service.
President Donald Trump also praised Giamanco, describing him as a "great hero" who "took care of business." Speaking to reporters at the White House, Trump said the shooting was a terrible tragedy but suggested the death toll could have been even higher without the father's intervention.
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," Trump said.
'The teacher shouted no, please'
Accounts from children who survived the attack have provided a harrowing picture of what unfolded inside the school.
Stacy Green, whose granddaughters, ages 7 and 11, attend Silver Rail Elementary, said the girls heard multiple gunshots coming from a neighboring classroom. They also heard a special education teacher pleading, "No, please," before more gunfire erupted.
Another grandmother, Christine Wenzke, said her 10-year-old grandson, Aizen, heard so many gunshots that he lost count. The boy, who was closest to his classroom door, rushed to lock it before joining his classmates and teacher behind lockers, following emergency procedures they had practiced.
"I locked the door and I went back behind our lockers," Aizen told ABC News. He said the students and their teacher were unharmed, but many children were terrified and crying.
Police identified one of the victims as 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert, remembered by her family as a compassionate educator devoted to children with special needs.
"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart," her family said in a statement. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs." Relatives also described her as a beloved daughter, sister, niece and granddaughter.
The youngest victim was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. His aunt, Swan Sheridan, remembered him as a fearless climber, a fast runner and an enthusiastic reader who adored his stuffed animals.
"He never met a stuffie that he didn't think needed to be rescued and cared for," she said. Sheridan described her nephew as a joyful child who had been full of energy since birth.
The names of the other two children killed, aged 8 and 11, were not released by police at their families' request. The two wounded victims, a 7-year-old student and teacher Becky Drury, remained under medical care. Authorities said the child was in serious but stable condition, while Drury's injuries were serious but not life-threatening.
A former student returns with a shotgun
The New York Times reported that the attacker had attended Silver Rail Elementary in 2020, when he was approximately 10 years old. His mother, Shauntai Nickerson, previously told a local news outlet that her son had struggled with remote learning during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Speaking to reporters after the shooting, Nickerson expressed grief for the families of the victims and said she wished she could have prevented the tragedy. Police said they were still investigating how the teenager obtained the shotgun and what motivated the attack.
Outside Silver Rail Elementary, residents of Bend have established a makeshift memorial filled with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals. Families and community members have gathered there to remember the victims and offer support to those affected.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter attends kindergarten at the school, told The Associated Press she was astonished that someone had been willing to pursue the gunman into the building. Fighting back tears, she described the intervention as extraordinary and said she was deeply grateful that more lives had been saved.
Silver Rail Elementary, located roughly 160 kilometers southeast of Portland, serves children from kindergarten through fifth grade and enrolled approximately 459 students last year. Classes across the Bend-La Pine school district were canceled Friday following the shooting.
As the community mourns the four victims, investigators continue trying to determine why a former student returned to his old elementary school armed with a shotgun. For the families of the children and teacher who died, and for the father who ran toward the gunfire, the events of those few minutes will leave a lasting mark.

sources.text:
The teen was a former student at Silver Rail Elementary School, officials said.
The 16-year-old gunman who opened fire inside a special needs classroom at Silver Rail Elementary School, killing three boys and a teacher was a former student at the Bend, Oregon school, investigators revealed Friday.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz identified the shooter Friday as Griffin John II, a Bend resident. The teenager made his way into the school Thursday afternoon with a Maverick 88 12-gauge pump-action shotgun and opened fire in the classroom after he shot at a truck outside of the school, Krantz told reporters at a news conference on Friday.
The chief did not immediately disclose how the shooter obtained the weapon.
"Currently, the origin of that possession is what we're working on," he said.
Preliminary information indicated the shotgun was believed to have been purchased by his mother, multiple sources told ABC News.
Krantz said a motive hadn't been immediately determined.
The police chief said the suspect was not currently enrolled in the school district but had previously attended Silver Rail.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook told reporters the shooter had been a special needs student during his time at the school.
Krantz said that search warrants were executed at the shooter's home and investigators are still combing through evidence and interviews.
"I think that's one of the most challenging parts of these types of investigations and cases is determining the why and the motives, and that that is part of the current very active, as I said, open investigation that we're working on," Krantz said.
"And it ... will require substantial investigative time to continue that. But that is the answer we're seeking as well. And as I've said before, we may never get that full answer, but we want it," he added.
The shooting began unfolding around 1 p.m. PT, when the teen threw the shotgun over a fence outside the school and then scaled it, Krantz said. A person in a truck that was nearby observed the shooter and verbally engaged the shooter, according to the chief.
The shooter fired at the truck, striking it at least three times, before he made his way into school, according to the chief.
The teenager shot through a door and made his way into a classroom before opening fire, Krantz said.
Krantz said that the shooter fired at least 15 rounds inside the classroom.
An unidentified teacher threw a phone at the suspect, tackled him and attempted to disarm him, according to the chief.
Another bystander, identified by his family as Kaylub Giamanco, saw the shooter enter the school while he was driving by, Krantz said.
He pursued the shooter and engaged him, fatally shooting him, Krantz said.
Giamanco has two daughters who attend the school and a concealed carry permit his family said.
Three boys, whose ages were 5, 8 and 11, were killed along with a teacher, Megan Lambert, 25, of Bend. The 5-year-old was identified Friday as Rhoam Summer.
An unidentified 7-year-old girl and Becky Drury, a 54-year-old teacher, were hospitalized with injuries, Krantz said.
The girl was in serious but stable condition, and Drury was being treated for serious but non-life-threatening injuries as of Friday afternoon, according to the chief.
Police are still going through the school but they said that the shooter had approximately 44 remaining rounds of ammunition on his person and in his backpack.

sources.news_title: What we know about the victims in the Bend, Oregon, elementary school shooting
sources.text:
The suspected shooter, a 16-year-old, was fatally shot.
The victims killed in a mass shooting at an Oregon elementary school included a teacher who was working her "dream job" and three students in a special needs classroom, officials said.
Another student and teacher were also injured in Thursday's shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, after a suspected 16-year-old gunman shot his way inside the school, police said.
All of the shooting victims were in a special needs classroom in the school, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said during a news conference on Friday.
Police identified one of the three students killed as 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. An 8-year-old boy and an 11-year-old boy also died, police said. Their names are not being released at the request of their families, according to Krantz.
Police identified the teacher killed in the shooting as 25-year-old Megan Lambert. Her family said Lambert was working her "dream job" at Silver Rail, in a statement read by a police official at the news conference.
"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart," the statement said. "She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs."
The family described her as "an incredible sister, daughter, niece, and granddaughter."
"Her friends became her family. She was funny and opinionated, and she lit up the room," the statement said.
Lambert grew up in Bend, played and coached volleyball and graduated from Boise State University in May 2023, according to the statement.
The other victims in the shooting included a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher, who were both taken to the hospital with critical injuries, police said. The child was in serious but stable condition on Friday, and the teacher -- identified by her family as Becky Drury -- suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said.
Drury's husband said they are currently focused on her recovery and "supporting our family through an unimaginably difficult time."
"We are incredibly grateful for the outpouring of support, prayers, and well-wishes following yesterday's tragedy at Silver Rail Elementary," her husband, Will Drury, said in a statement. "The kindness and concern shown to our family and everyone affected mean more than we can express. We live in a truly special community."
"We ask that you continue to hold everyone affected by this tragedy in your thoughts," he added.
The suspected shooter was fatally shot by a community member who saw the teen going into the Silver Rail Elementary School after firing at a truck in front of the building, Krantz said.
In another "heroic" act that may have saved lives, the police chief said another teacher tackled the shooter to the floor and tried to take the gun away from him. That teacher was not injured, police said.
A motive in the shooting remains under investigation, police said. The suspect had attended the elementary school as a special needs student and was not currently enrolled in the school district, officials said.
Editor's Note: Police have corrected their initial spelling of the 25-year-old teacher's name. The correct spelling is Megan Lambert.

sources.news_title: Oregon school shooter was former special needs student, police say
sources.text:
Oregon school shooter was former special needs student, police say
A teacher fought the teenage shooter and a parent shot him dead, police say on Friday, a day after four people were killed.
The 16-year-old who killed three children and a teacher at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon was a former special-needs student at the school, police and school officials have said.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz identified the attacker on Friday, a day after the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, as Griffin J. John II.
He said the teenager attacked a classroom of special-needs students, where all the victims were shot.
Steven Cook, superintendent of Bend-La Pine Schools, said John was not enrolled in the local public school system at the time.
“That classroom was a special needs classroom, and the suspect was a special needs student in that school,” Cook told a news conference.
Krantz said John shot his way through locked doors with a 12-gauge shotgun, firing as many as 15 shots, and had about 44 rounds left when he was killed. Police are still trying to determine how he obtained the gun.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or with a parent’s consent.
The shooter’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, separately told reporters outside her apartment: “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something.”
A teacher threw her phone at the gunman, then tackled and fought him, likely saving lives, Krantz said, calling her actions “heroic”. She was not injured.
A 36-year-old father, Kaylub Giamanco, who has two children at the school, then followed the gunman inside and shot him dead minutes after the first 911 call.
US President Donald Trump called Giamanco a “great hero”. “It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump said.
The children killed were aged five, eight and 11, and the teacher was Meghan Lambert, 25, police said.
A seven-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were taken to hospital in critical condition.
The shooting is the 28th mass killing in the US this year, according to a database by The Associated Press, USA Today and Northeastern University.
The Gun Violence Archive in the US has documented 369 mass shootings in 2026, defined as incidents in which four or more people are shot.
The Everytown for Gun Safety group has counted at least 100 incidents of gunfire on school grounds this year, with 34 deaths.

sources.news_title: 'Hero' bystanders helped prevent further bloodshed in Oregon shooting
sources.text:
'Hero' bystanders helped prevent further bloodshed in deadly Oregon school shooting
In short:
Police have hailed a father and a teacher who intervened in a school shooting that claimed the lives of four people, including children, as heroes.
Investigators have released new information about the teenage shooter, who has been identified as a former student at the elementary school.
What's next?
Police continue to investigate the 16-year-old's background and possible motives.
Authorities investigating the fatal shooting that claimed the lives of three children and a teacher in Oregon have hailed a father and a teacher who intervened as heroes.
Speaking to the media a day after the tragic shooting at an elementary school in Bend, Police Chief Mike Krantz praised the actions of several bystanders who "intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse".
"We owe you a debt of gratitude," he said.
Chief Krantz said the 16-year-old shooter, identified as Griffin J John II, a former special-needs student at Silver Rail Elementary, was shot dead by a man whose children also attend the school in Bend.
Police say just before 1pm on Thursday, local time, the teen was observed throwing a gun over the school's gates and scaling the fence.
Chief Krantz said a witness confronted the gunman, who shot a number of rounds at their car before continuing towards the school. The witness called 911 shortly after.
A 36-year-old father with two children attending the school witnessed the initial shooting and pursued the teen armed with his "legally secured" pistol, Chief Krantz said.
He entered the school and found the 16-year-old struggling with another teacher before firing multiple rounds at the teen, killing him.
The police chief did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, but told the press conference she threw her phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.
"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Chief Krantz said.
Initial investigations have determined the teen had gained entry into the school by shooting the glass panes in the doors.
He went into a classroom, identified as a special-needs class, and fired up to 15 rounds using a 12-gauge pump-action shotgun, killing three children and one adult.
"All of the victims were shot in that classroom," Chief Krantz told reporters.
A 25-year-old teacher from Oregon, Meghan Lambert, was identified as the adult killed in the shooting.
Her family said she had found her "dream job" in a statement provided to police and read to reporters at a press conference on Friday.
In the statement, they described her as funny and opinionated and said she "lit up the room."
"Meghan was compassionate and had a huge heart," her family said in the statement.
"Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher," they said.
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.
"Meghan loved those children."
The youngest victim, identified with the permission of his family, was five-year-old Rhoam Summer.
The boy's aunt, Swan Sheridan, said Rhoam was a "happy" child who loved his stuffed animals and "creatures that were, in his words, 'misunderstood,'" she said.
Ms Sheridan said her nephew would climb and jump off anything and was an "incredibly fast" runner, even from a young age.
"He was a little ball of energy from the moment he was born,"
she said.
"He was a very, very happy child," she said.
Two boys aged eight and 11 were also killed.
A seven-year-old girl remains in a serious but stable condition, while a 54-year-old female teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries.
Chief Krantz said police are yet to confirm a motive and how the 16-year-old came into possession of the gun.
He said a further 45 rounds of ammunition were found in a backpack belonging to the teen and found nearby.
Holding back tears, he said: "Please hold the victims of this tragedy, the families and your community in your hearts with me."

sources.news_title: Silver Rail Elementary School Shooter Identified as Griffin John; Father Who Intervened is Kaylub Giamanco - The Source - Bend, Oregon
sources.text:
Authorities have identified Griffin J. John II as the suspect in the Oct. 15 shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School that resulted in the deaths of three children and a teacher, and the critical injuries of another teacher and student.
Speaking at a press conference Friday afternoon at Bend Municipal Court, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told a scrum of local and national reporters that he would “only say the shooter’s name once.” Krantz said John arrived at the school on foot, yet the exact route is a part of the open and active investigation.
In the special needs classroom, the first and last classroom John entered during his shooting spree, the 16-year-old shooter was shot several times by an armed bystander, who’d pursued John into the school after witnessing the 16-year-old shooting at a previous witness, driving a red truck, who’d confronted him. That initial bystander was not injured, authorities said.
The bystander, 36, told investigators he heard shooting and saw the shooter struggling with a teacher, who’d thrown her phone at the attacker and tackled him. That teacher was uninjured, police said.
Krantz declined to name the bystander who shot and killed John in the special needs classroom, only stating the good Samaritan, who was not injured, fired his legal .40 caliber pistol several times at John, killing him.
The man’s mother, however, identified the bystander as Kaylub Giamanco, while making a statement on Friday. Giamanco is the father of two Silver Rail students and lives a few blocks from the school.
“He is not seeking recognition,” Kenda Freeman said, reading the statement from her phone. “But instead wishes to express gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support.”
Investigators serviced a search warrant of John’s home; police declined to say whether his parents were cooperative with the investigation. They also declined to confirm early reports that the gun had been purchased by John’s mother.
The gun that John used in the shooting is a Maverick 88 12-gauge. Krantz said John fired three types of ammunition: bird and buck shot and slugs. The shooter was able to enter the locked school doors by shooting out the locks, Krantz said. In John’s backpack and on his person, authorities recovered 44 additional slugs and cartridges.
A Bend PD school resource officer, who’s responsible for the safety of six or seven additional Bend-La Pine schools, was at a nearby school at the time of the Silver Rails shooting, police said.
Authorities will relinquish the crime scene in Silver Rail on Oct. 20, but Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said the school district will stay closed for an undetermined amount of time. Cook told the Source that where Silver Rail students would resume the school year is unclear at this time.
The school district practices live shooter drills twice a year, Cook said.
“Rest assured,” Cook added. “We will take a hard look at everything and what we have done, and what more needs to be done to ensure that our students, our staff, and our families are safe in our schools.”
Victims and survivors
Authorities gave updates on the conditions of the two injured. The 54-year-old teacher is being treated at St. Charles Medical Center with serious but not life-threatening injuries. Her family gave authorities permission to identify her as Bend resident Becky Drury. A 7-year-old student is in stable condition while receiving care at OHSU.
At the request of the family, authorities identified Rhoam Summer as the 5-year-old boy killed in the shooting. The other child victims were ages 8 and 11. As of press time, more than $104,000 had been raised for the Summer family on the crowd-funding site Meal Train.
Among those killed was Megan Lambert, a Silver Rail educational assistant. Lambert had worked as a substitute teacher at the school before recently being hired full time. It was “her dream job,” the Lambert family wrote in a statement read by the authorities.
Lambert also coached with Central Oregon Volleyball Club. The club’s online about-page, features a tribute to each coach. Lambert’s reads: “Coach Megan is truly a blessing and did so much for her team! Megan pushes her team to be their very best and is committed to their success and growth throughout the season! Megan puts her whole heart into her team!”
Lambert also has a connection with the Source. In 2017, while a student at Mountain View High School, she interned with our newsroom, doing photography and other tasks, including helping with the Source’s 20th anniversary issue, for which she was mentioned in a Source Instagram post in August 2017.
An online petition, calling for Giamanco to be granted the key to the city by the Bend City Council and Mayor Melanie Kebler — “if and when he and his family are ready to accept it” — was launched Friday afternoon by Jacob Derman, a local attorney with no relation to Giamanco.
At a press conference hours after the Oct. 15 shooting, Gov. Tina Kotek said her thoughts were with Giamanco, calling his actions heroic. President Donald Trump echoed that sentiment at a press conference Friday.
Sheila Miller, the Bend PD spokesperson, confirmed that Griffin is the shooter’s first name, not last, as misreported previously by national outlets such as CNN and The New York Times.
Authorities urge those with tips regarding the Silver Rail shooting to contact the FBI hotline: 1-800-CALL FBI or visit fbi.gov/silverrailschool
A note from Bend PD:
We are asking the public for their assistance in helping us determine how the suspect got to Silver Rail Elementary School. Please review any video footage you may have from between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15. We are looking for video evidence specifically in the area between Third Street and Brosterhous Road, as well as in the area of Silver Rail Elementary School, of a teenage male, approximately 6 feet tall and 140 pounds, wearing black pants, a black T-shirt and a black backpack. If you find video that you believe is helpful, you can follow this link https://bendpdor.evidence.com/axon/community-request/public/silverrail and submit it.
Griffin was a sick boy. Sicker are those who perpetuate needless and reckless ownership of firepower in this country.

sources.news_title: Teacher, 25, killed in Oregon shooting identified
Slain Bend teacher Megan Lambert, armed dad deemed heros, police say
sources.text:
BEND, Ore. - Bend Police released new details about the shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School that left five people dead, including three children and a teacher.
According to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, the attack happened just before 1 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15.
"Yesterday was a terrible day for our community, and I appreciate the thousands of people who showed up at last night's vigil at Drake Park because you care about each other, and that mattered," Krantz said. "That is what community looks like."
Police said the shooter, 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, approached the school from an undeveloped area near Nina Avenue around 12:58 p.m. He threw his weapon over the fence and climbed onto school property. A driver in a red Toyota pickup truck saw this and confronted him, but the shooter fired at the truck, hitting it at least three times.
A 36-year-old man whose children attend the school also witnessed the shooting. He drove into the school parking lot, grabbed a legally secured 40-caliber pistol from his car and entered the building through the doors the shooter had forced open. The shooter had walked along the south side of the school and fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of double doors to get inside. He went directly into the classroom to the left of the entry doors and fired as many as 15 rounds. All victims were shot in that classroom.
Inside, a teacher tackled the shooter and fought to take the firearm from him. The 36-year-old man saw the teacher in a physical fight with the shooter and fired his weapon, striking the shooter multiple times. The teacher who tackled the shooter was not hurt.
Five people died at the scene, including the shooter. The victims include three boys, ages 5, 8 and 11, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert of Bend. The 5-year-old has been identified as Rhoam Summer at his family's request.
A 7-year-old girl and 54-year-old teacher Becky Drury were taken to the hospital with critical injuries. The girl is now at OHSU in serious but stable condition. Drury suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries and is at St. Charles Bend.
Police said the shooter used three types of ammunition during the attack: 12-gauge birdshot, buckshot and slugs. Officers found a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun near the shooter, along with a backpack. He had about 44 remaining rounds of 12-gauge ammunition on him or in the backpack.
The shooter previously attended Silver Rail Elementary but is not currently enrolled in Bend-La Pine Schools. Police believe he walked to the school, but the route is still under investigation. How he got the weapon and ammunition is part of the active criminal investigation.
Officers arrived at the scene at 1:02 p.m., just three minutes after the first 911 call. The school went into lockdown at 1:01 p.m. All students and staff were taken by school buses to Journey Church to meet with their families.
Roughly 150 law enforcement and first responder personnel have been involved in the investigation. Police completed a digital scan of the entire scene and executed a search warrant at the shooter's home. Officers do not plan to release the scene until Tuesday of next week at the earliest.
Lambert's family released a statement describing her as a native Central Oregonian who grew up in Bend and graduated from Mountain View High School in 2019. She graduated from Boise State in May 2023 and traveled to Barcelona, Spain with TEFL Iberia. Silver Rail was her first job as a teacher, though she had subbed there for many years through High Desert ESD.
"She LOVED Silver Rail - this was her dream job," the family said. "Megan was compassionate and had a huge heart. She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs."
The family thanked the man who intervened. "We want the bystander who intervened to know we know he is going through a rough time, but we are grateful and we think he is a hero," the family said. "You selflessly put yourself at risk for others."
Police are asking the public to review any video footage from between 10 a.m. and 1 p.m. on Thursday, Oct. 15. They are looking for video of a teenage male, about 6 feet tall and 140 pounds, wearing black pants, a black T-shirt and a black backpack in the area between Third Street and Brosterhous Road, as well as near Silver Rail Elementary School. People can submit video at bendpdor.evidence.com/axon/community-request/public/silverrail.
The FBI has set up a tipline for the incident at 1-800-CALL-FBI or at the FBI's website.

sources.news_title: Oregon school attack: Teen shooter was former student, police say
sources.text:
A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said on Friday (October 16, 2026).
City of Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called the teacher's actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
Authorities said John had been a special needs student at Silver Rail Elementary and had attacked a classroom with special needs students. He fired as many as 15 shots from a 12-gauge shotgun and had about 44 rounds remaining when he was killed, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” he said. “We may never get that full answer, but we want it.”
The police chief added that police are also still trying to determine how the shooter obtained the gun.
The attacker’s mother, Shauntai Nickerson, told reporters outside her apartment near the school that if she could have done something to prevent the shooting, she would have.
“I miss my boy,” Ms. Nickerson said, sobbing and crying, according to The New York Times and CNN. “I’m so sorry, I wish I could have done something. I’m sorry for their loss.”
She declined to say how the 16-year-old obtained the pump-action shotgun and didn’t comment further when The Associated Press and other outlets knocked on her apartment door later.
In a 2020 interview with the local news station KTVZ, Ms. Nickerson identified the boy, then 10, as a participant in a special needs program run by the school district. It was called NEST, for Nurturing Empathy, Safety and Trust, and aimed at helping students experiencing intensive behavioural and social skill challenges. Ms. Nickerson said he struggled trying to learn from home during the pandemic.
How the events unfolded
The first 911 call came from the driver of a red pickup truck early Thursday afternoon who saw the boy throw his gun over a fence outside the school and then climb over it, Mr. Krantz said. The driver yelled at the boy, who fired at him, striking the truck three times. The driver was not injured, but drove off and called for help.
A second driver, a 36-year-old man whose children attend Silver Rail, saw John shooting at the truck and heading toward the school. He pulled into the parking lot, grabbed his .40-caliber pistol and followed the attacker inside. He saw John wrestling with the teacher and shot him several times, Mr. Krantz said.
Police found John dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Mr. Krantz said. John shot through locked doors to get inside, police said.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Mr. Krantz said. Three children ages 5, 8 and 11, and teacher Meghan Lambert, 25, were killed, police said. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, Krantz said.
The youngest victim was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born.”
The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery.
The pump-action shotgun the attacker used was bought by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Mass killings this year
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.
U.S. President Donald Trump on Friday praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Mr. Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.

sources.news_title: 'Undoubtedly saved people': teacher fought US shooter
sources.text:
'Undoubtedly saved people': teacher fought US shooter
A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult threw her mobile phone at the shooter, tackled him and fought him in an act that saved lives, police say.
A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, authorities released new details of the scene inside a special needs classroom of Silver Rail Elementary School where three school children aged five, eight and 11 and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, but told a press conference she threw her phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.
"She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed," Krantz said.
As the two wrestled, a parent entered the classroom and opened fire on the gunman, killing him.
Officials said the parent had followed the shooter into the school, upon witnessing him firing a shotgun from just outside campus. By the time police arrived within three minutes of receiving their first call, the shooter was dead, police said.
In the meantime the 16-year-old assailant, who had shot through locked glass doors to enter campus, had killed four people and wounded two others.
Krantz, speaking to the heroism shown by the teacher who threw herself onto the suspect and the parent who shot him, said, "I don't think we can underestimate or under-appreciate that courage. When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognise that."
He said the bystander's actions "undoubtedly saved people," and "the teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that's true heroism."
Krantz identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, who was armed with 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him.
The parent who killed the shooter was identified as Kaylub Giamanco, his mother told the New York Times. She identified him as the father of two girls who attend the school, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.
"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," Freeman said.
Residents of Bend, a city of about 100,000 people some 280km southeast of Portland, gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles just outside yellow crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene.
"Thank God for that father. He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today. We wish him well, and thank God for him," Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears.
Such school shootings have become common in the US, with each one reviving debates over gun laws in a country where a right to "keep and bear Arms" is protected under the Constitution's Second Amendment.

sources.text:
Teacher fought US school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
- Published
Some readers may find this article distressing.
A female teacher in the US state of Oregon tackled a teenage shooter who entered her classroom and tried to wrestle the gun from his grasp, police have said.
The teacher, who has not been named, threw her mobile phone before trying to disarm the 16-year-old on the floor of a classroom at Silver Rail Elementary in the city of Bend.
The attacker killed three children and a teacher after shooting his way into the building on Thursday.
He was shot dead by a father with two daughters at the school, who was driving past as the attack started to unfold and, armed with a pistol, ran in to confront the suspect.
Police said the attacker used to be a student at the school. His motive remains unclear.
He had been armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped, police said. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
"To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude," Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said.
Police used a news conference on Friday to identify two of the four victims of the school shooting. They were five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
Lambert's family said in a statement shared by the police that her goal was to be a teacher in the district in which she grew up and that she was "compassionate and had a huge heart".
"She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs," they said.
Bryan Jolly, Summer's grandfather, said the family was devastated by his death.
"The whole thing is senseless, and a shock," he told the New York Times, saying his grandson was "was very bright and very mischievous and very fun-loving, and totally without fear".
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school had saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman had not been hurt but "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed".
Krantz identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who had been a special educational needs student at the school.
A search warrant has been executed at his home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco's family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school and then shoot through a window to gain entry.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle, while his brother said he grabbed the pistol "and decided to go in after" the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect "multiple times", killing him.
Giamanco's mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station that her son had called her moments after the shooting and that he was "traumatised".
"He said 'a man went into my daughter's school'," Freeman recalled, pausing as she started to tear up. "And, um, shot kids. And he said, 'and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mum'."
She added: "I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, 'mum, I couldn't save them all'."
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a "great hero" and telling reporters that the situation could have become "much worse".
"It's a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it," he said.
Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man's heroic actions as having stopped further loss of life, but noted they "carry a heavy emotional burden and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well".

sources.text:
BEND, Ore. — A teacher threw her phone at the teenage gunman who killed four people at an Oregon elementary school, then tackled and fought with him — likely saving lives before he was shot by a father who followed him into the building, police said Friday.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz called her actions “heroic” during a news conference and said she was not injured. He identified the attacker as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at the school, and said all of the victims were shot in the same classroom.
In a statement read to reporters on Friday, Kenda Freeman said her son, Kaylub Giamanco, shot the gunman in Thursday’s attack at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend. She said he is the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, noting that her son is a lifelong resident of Bend, a mountain-ringed city of about 100,000 in central Oregon.
She said her family was asking for privacy “during this difficult time.”
The youngest victim, just 5 years old, was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born.”
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Gov. Tina Kotek — without naming Giamanco — said he had followed the gunman into the school and helped end the rampage as police began arriving.
“Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening," Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. "I’m feeling very grateful.”
The attacker's mom bought the gun he used
The shooter was found dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. He shot through locked doors to get inside, police said.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said Thursday.
The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a tourism and outdoor recreation hub that has ballooned in population and sits about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.

By Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom
BEND, Oregon, Oct 16 (Reuters) – A 16-year-old boy who shot and killed a teacher and three children in an Oregon special-needs classroom was stopped by another teacher who tackled him and an armed father who fatally shot him, officials said on Friday.
Their actions on Thursday saved other lives, the local police chief told a press conference.
A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, police released new details of the scene at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, where three schoolchildren aged 5, 8 and 11 were killed along with 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
A 7-year-old was wounded and listed in serious but stable condition, and another teacher suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said.
The unidentified teacher who stopped the shooter on Thursday threw her phone at him, tackled and fought him. A 36-year-old father of two students then rushed in with a legal .40-caliber pistol and fired at the suspect multiple times, killing him just before police arrived.
This teacher, who was not injured, “almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz, at times choking back emotion, told a press conference.
“The teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that’s true heroism,” he said, without identifying her.
Kenda Freeman told the New York Times that her son Kaylub Giamanco, whose two daughters attend the school, killed the shooter, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.
“He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support,” Freeman said, adding that he asked for privacy and did not want to speak to the media.
Officials identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, a 16-year-old former special-needs student at the school who was armed with a 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him, police said.
Police were trying to determine what motivated the shooter and how he obtained a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun, Krantz said.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us … We may never get that full answer, but we want it,” the police chief said.
Just before the shooting, the assailant was seen throwing his weapon over the school fence and then climbing after it onto school grounds. The driver of a truck passing by at the time verbally confronted the boy, who opened fire on the vehicle.
The assailant shot through locked glass doors and stormed a class of mixed-grade special-needs students. Police arrived within three minutes of the first call, and the shooter was already dead, Krantz said.
VICTIMS MOURNED
People in Bend, a city of about 100,000 some 175 miles (280 km) southeast of Portland, gathered near the school to mourn on Friday morning, placing flowers and candles outside yellow crime scene tape that cordoned off the scene.
“Thank God for that father,” Michael Zappa, 71, who lives just blocks from the school, said through tears. “He saved a lot of lives yesterday, and our prayers should go out for him because he has a lot on his mind today.”
The family of the slain teacher, Lambert, said working at Silver Rail was a “dream job” for her.
“She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs,” the family said in a statement that was read aloud at Friday’s news conference.
Lambert’s family also praised Giamanco and expressed gratitude to him.
“We think he is a hero,” the family said, according to the statement.
US school shootings have become more frequent in recent years. Since the start of this year, 118 people have been wounded or killed in 149 incidents involving a gun fired or brandished in a school, or gunshots striking school property, according to the K-12 School Shooting Database, a nonprofit online tracker.
A separate online database, the Gun Violence Archive, has recorded 371 mass shootings since January 2026, defining mass shootings as four or more people being struck by gunfire, not including the shooter. Three of those, including the Bend incident, occurred in public schools, the archive said.
(Reporting by Herbert Villarraga and Deborah Bloom in Bend; Additional reproting by Jonathan Allen in New York and Steve Gorman in Los Angeles; Writing by Daniel Trotta; Editing by Paul Thomasch, Jonathan Spicer, Sergio Non and Cynthia Osterman)

Three Children, Teacher Killed In Latest US School Shooting; Community Prays For Victims
by Stefan J. Bos, Worthy News Chief International Correspondent
BEND, USA (Worthy News) – Parents waited anxiously to be reunited with their children, while hundreds of residents gathered for prayers and a candlelight vigil after a teenage gunman killed three young students and a teacher at an elementary school in the northwestern United States.
The children, ages 5, 8, and 11, were killed Thursday at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, a city in central Oregon, about 175 miles (280 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
A 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were critically wounded and rushed to St. Charles Medical Center, U.S. authorities said. The victims’ names were not immediately released.
The suspected gunman, a 16-year-old boy, was shot and killed by a community member who pursued him into the school and confronted him, police said.
The attack was the latest in a series of deadly school shootings in the United States, renewing concerns about the safety of children and teachers in American classrooms.
PARENTS WAIT FOR CHILDREN
As police evacuated classrooms, anxious families gathered at a nearby church, where students and staff were taken to be reunited with their loved ones.
Among them was Drew Sharp, whose son attended fifth grade at the school. He described how younger children were brought off the buses first, prolonging his anxious wait for his son.
Another local resident, Erin Johnson, said she heard what sounded like gunfire while visiting her parents near the school.
She recalled hearing a neighbor scream as police vehicles rushed toward the building.
The neighbor’s children attended Silver Rail and were later confirmed safe.
Johnson expressed grief for the young victims, describing them simply as “babies.”
FEARING THE WORST
Irvin Ornelas, whose 10-year-old brother attended the school, said he believed he saw the gunman heading toward the building.
“I saw him throw his gun over and him jump over the fence very quickly,” Ornelas recalled.
His brother survived unharmed, but Ornelas said he feared the worst as the emergency unfolded.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the violence began shortly before 1 p.m. Thursday when emergency dispatchers received a call from someone reporting that a person armed with a long gun had fired several shots at their vehicle.
Dispatchers subsequently received dozens of calls reporting that the gunman had entered Silver Rail Elementary School.
GUNMAN FORCES ENTRY
Investigators said the teenager forced his way through locked doors by shooting at them, raising questions about the effectiveness of security measures intended to protect students and teachers.
Police officers arrived within three minutes of the first emergency call, but the attacker had already been fatally shot.
“An officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz told reporters.
Officers entering the building subsequently discovered the bodies of the four victims and provided emergency assistance to the wounded.
Authorities did not immediately identify the gunman or establish a motive. Investigators were also examining whether the teenager had any connection to the school.
WEAPON UNDER INVESTIGATION
Law enforcement sources familiar with the investigation said the attacker used a shotgun. A law enforcement official briefed on the case said it was a pump-action shotgun reportedly purchased by the suspect’s mother.
Police had not publicly confirmed the precise type of firearm used or disclosed how many shots were fired during the attack.
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF), and Oregon State Police joined local authorities in investigating the shooting.
FBI Director Kash Patel said federal agents were assisting the investigation, which included efforts to establish how the teenager obtained the weapon.
Oregon Governor Tina Kotek praised the unidentified community member who confronted the attacker, saying the person’s actions had “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life.”
GOVERNOR PRAISES COURAGE
Kotek acknowledged that such an intervention also carried a heavy emotional burden.
“All Oregonians mourn this loss today,” Kotek said during a news briefing. “This is a horrible day. No parent should have to have this kind of day. And no community should have to live through this kind of day.”
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook struggled to describe the devastation confronting families and educators.
“Today an unthinkable tragedy happened at Silver Rail Elementary School,” he told reporters.
“No community should have to do what we are doing right now. I don’t have any words for what this community is feeling right now.”
PRAYERS AND CANDLELIGHT VIGIL
As darkness fell Thursday, hundreds of residents gathered at Drake Park in Bend for a candlelight vigil honoring those killed and wounded.
Local religious leaders joined residents in offering prayers, while mourners sang songs and remembered the victims.
Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler, herself the mother of an elementary school student, acknowledged the profound grief gripping the community.
Flowers, balloons, and candles were also left outside the school as residents struggled to comprehend the loss of three children and a teacher.

The shooting occurred at Silver Rail Elementary School.
By Meredith Deliso, Jack Moore, and Nadine El-Bawab
The mass shooting at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school on Thursday that left three children and one teacher dead took place inside a special needs classroom, authorities said at a news conference, identifying some of the victims and the suspected shooter.
Three boys, ages 5, 8 and 11, and the teacher died at the scene, police said. At a news conference on Friday, authorities identified the teacher as 25-year-old Megan Lambert, and one of the boys as 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. The names of the other two children killed are not being released at the request of their families, police said.
The suspected shooter, a 16-year-old armed with a twelve-gauge shotgun, was fatally shot by a community member who saw the teen going into the Silver Rail Elementary School and pursued him inside, according to Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz.
In another "heroic" act that may have saved lives, he said another teacher tackled the shooter to the floor and tried to take the gun away from him.
A 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded in the gunfire and were taken to the hospital with critical injuries, police said. The child was in serious but stable condition on Friday, and the teacher -- identified by her family as Becky Drury -- suffered serious but non-life-threatening injuries, police said.
Police identified the suspected shooter on Friday as Griffin J. John II, a Bend resident who formerly attended Silver Rail Elementary School. The suspect had been a special needs student at the school, school officials confirmed. He was not currently enrolled in the school district, according to the police chief.
Preliminary information indicates the 16-year-old suspected shooter used a pump-action shotgun believed to be purchased by his mother, multiple sources told ABC News.
"How the suspect got the weapon and ammunition remains part of the active criminal investigation, and I will not be able to address any of that portion today," Krantz said at a press briefing on Friday.
A motive also remains under investigation, police said.
"It will require substantial investigative time to continue that, but that is the answer we're seeking as well," Krantz said. "We may never get that full answer, but we want it."
How the shooting unfolded
The incident began unfolding shortly before 1 p.m. PT Thursday, police said.
At 12:59 p.m., police received a call from a driver who reported being shot at multiple times by a person with a long gun, the police chief said. The vehicle was struck three times.
Shortly afterward, the Deschutes County dispatch center began receiving multiple 911 calls that a shooter had entered Silver Rail Elementary School. The school was directed to go into lockdown at 1:01 p.m, Krantz said.
The shooter "forced" his way inside the school by shooting at the glass panes of locked doors multiple times, according to the police chief.
"The suspect went directly into the classroom, immediately to the left of the entry doors, where he fired as many as 15 rounds overall," Krantz said.
Officers arrived on the scene at 1:02 p.m., police said.
All of the shooting victims were located in that special needs classroom, he said. The suspect was also shot in the classroom and died at the scene, he said.
A Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun was located near the suspect, who had approximately 44 remaining rounds of 12-gauge ammunition, according to the chief.
