Police said the shooter was fatally shot inside the classroom by a 36-year-old community member who had seen the teen firing at the truck and then followed him into the school, Krantz said.
His family on Friday identified him as Kaylub Giamanco, a father with two daughters who attend Silver Rail Elementary School.
Giamanco -- a lifelong Bend resident -- was driving near the school when he heard the commotion and ran inside, according to his family, who said he regrets not being able to save more lives. His family confirmed he has a concealed carry permit.
"He is not seeking recognition, but instead wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support," the Giamanco family said in a statement.
Police also commended another teacher who threw her cellphone at the shooter after he entered the classroom. The police chief said the teacher then "tackled him and fought to take the firearm from him," and that she "almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed." The police chief did not identify the teacher, and noted that she was uninjured.
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek thanked teachers, staff and first responders who rushed to the scene and thanked the community member who she said "heroically intervened to stop further loss of life."

Following the shooting, police said they evacuated the school room by room. A reunification site for families was set up at a nearby church.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook called the shooting an "unthinkable tragedy" and said, "We are heartbroken. We are horrified."
Thousands of community members gathered for a candlelight vigil Thursday night at Drake Park in Bend. A makeshift memorial has also grown outside the elementary school, with mourners leaving flowers, candles, toys and stuffed animals.
Kotek ordered flags at Oregon public institutions to be flown at half-staff on Friday from sunrise to sunset in remembrance of those who lost their lives at Silver Rail Elementary School.
Classes, activities and athletic events at all Bend-La Pine Schools were canceled Friday, school officials said.
"A school should be a safe place where children can learn and feel secure. What happened today should never happen," Bend Mayor Melanie Kebler said at Thursday's press briefing. "Like so many in our community, I'm struggling to make sense of a loss that feels unimaginable."
Large police response
A school resource officer was not at the elementary school at the time of the shooting, a police spokesperson said, noting that he officer oversees multiple schools and was at a nearby campus at the time.
The shooting sparked a large police presence as law enforcement and first responders raced to the school. Over 150 law enforcement officers and first responders have been involved in the investigation, police said.
"Everything they were doing seemed highly trained and highly prepared for this," Caleb Weis, who was riding his motorcycle near the school at the time, told ABC News.
"I didn't see as many phones out recording as you see on many other occasions, just a kind of a shock factor and an immense amount of respect for the law enforcement, first responders," he said.
FBI Director Kash Patel said the agency was on the scene assisting in the investigation. Agents with the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives were also responding, according to a source.
Some parents who heard the sirens came to the school and anxiously awaited information.
"There's really no way to prepare for something like this," one father told ABC Bend affiliate KOHD.
ABC News' Alyssa Pone and Lisa Sivertsen contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: A Shooting Strikes an Elementary School. Some Doubt Policy Change Will Follow
sources.text:
The community in Bend, Ore., was left reeling this week after a 16-year-old shot and killed three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in the Bend-La Pine district. A 7-year-old and another teacher were also critically injured.
The child victims, ages 5, 8, and 11, include the youngest person killed in a school shooting since Education Week began tracking these incidents in 2018.
Of the 267 shootings Education Week has tracked in those years, at least 20 have been at elementary schools.
When such young children are the victims, outrage and calls for change tend to intensify, said Jaclyn Schildkraut, the executive director of the Regional Gun Violence Research Consortium at the Rockefeller Institute of Government in Albany, N.Y. She’s researched policy responses to school shootings.
“What happened yesterday, with the age of these children, brings us right back to 2012 with Sandy Hook,” Schildkraut said, referencing the shooting in Newtown, Conn., in which a 20-year-old shot and killed 20 first grade children and six staff members.
“There tends to be a lot of outcry: If we’re not protecting our most vulnerable, then who are we protecting?”
A chorus of state leaders has begun to call for action since Thursday’s shooting. But some observers fear that while the death of elementary-age children may prompt fury and powerful statements, it won’t spur real change that could stop future school shootings.
Kevin Lein was the principal of Harrisburg High School in Harrisburg, S.D., when a 16-year-old student shot him in his office in 2015. In the years since, Lein has advocated for legislation to prevent the deadly attacks.
He is a founding member of the National Principals Association’s Principal Recovery Network, a support and advocacy group for school leaders who have survived school shootings.
“When Uvalde happened, we thought, ‘This has to make a change,’” said Lein, referencing the 2022 shooting at Robb Elementary School in Uvalde, Texas, when an 18-year-old former student shot and killed 19 students and two teachers.
“When Sandy Hook happened, ‘This has to make a change,’” he continued. “And it doesn’t.”
Calls for ‘harder’ schools likely to emerge, some say
Shootings, especially in elementary schools, can reignite political will for policy change, said Schildkraut. Often, the policy movement happens at the local level.
“Obviously, there was a lot of change in Connecticut after Sandy Hook,” she said. “There was a lot of change in Texas after Uvalde. There’s going to be pressure.”
In Texas, lawmakers passed several measures aimed at bolstering school safety in the years after the shooting at Robb Elementary, training school personnel, increasing the presence of armed security officers, strengthening emergency response, and providing mental health resources.
Some Uvalde parents pushed for stricter gun laws, too, but legislative proposals died in the face of Republican opposition.
The Uvalde shooting did prompt federal legislative action, but the resulting bill—the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act—focused more on school mental health services and student safety measures than gun restrictions.
On Friday, Sandy Hook Promise, a nonprofit organization advocating against gun violence that formed after the Sandy Hook shooting, issued a statement calling in part for stronger gun control.
“What I cannot accept is that we keep allowing this to be the story of childhood in America,” said Sandy Hook Promise co-founder and CEO Nicole Hockley, in the statement.
“Preventing tragedy means securing firearms from unauthorized access, recognizing the early warning signs of a young person in crisis, making it safe to speak up, ensuring someone is ready to respond, and intervening long before a crisis turns deadly.”
In the aftermath of the Bend shooting, it’s also likely that some policymakers and advocates will call for “harder” schools that add more barriers to entry, said Ken Trump, president of National School Safety and Security Services, a consulting firm that works with districts.
In Thursday’s attack, the shooter forced his way into Silver Rail Elementary by shooting at locked doors, according to an AP report.
“People are going to clamor for increased physical security,” Trump said. But the best security measures are often “less visible,” he said, referencing staff training in situational awareness and how to make difficult decisions under stress.
Lein voiced a similar perspective.
“We keep talking about hardening. How is it working out for us? It isn’t; he shot through the door,” he said, referencing the Bend incident.
Authorities said the incident at the Oregon school could have been worse had it not been for the intervention of a man who shot the assailant.
On Friday, the mother of the man who intervened said he was the father of two girls at the school.
“He is not seeking recognition,” the mother, Kenda Freeman, said of her son, identified as Kaylub Giamanco. He instead “wishes to express his gratitude to the first responders, school personnel, and community for the outpouring of love and support.”
Option of Arming Educators Has Mixed Support
In the wake of previous school some shootings, some have called for arming educators.
As of 2025, at least 29 states allowed schools to arm teachers or other staff, not just school resource officers, according to an analysis from the RAND Corporation.
It’s a controversial approach. The majority of teachers oppose the policy, though a substantial minority of American adults—45 percent—say they are in favor of the idea.
Last year, lawmakers in a handful of states introduced legislation aimed at addressing some of the “human factors” in school security, like training, threat assessment, and encouraging students to report concerns about potential violence.
When state lawmakers ask districts to put in place new policies to bolster school safety, schools need continued support and funding to maintain that work, long after the news cycle about a shooting ends, said Denise Fredericks, the principal of Townville Elementary School in Townville, S.C., and another member of the Principal Recovery Network.
“Whatever we’ve done, we’ve got to sustain,” she said.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

The youngest victim, just 5 years old, was a fast runner and fearless climber who loved reading and his stuffed animals, his aunt said Friday.
“He never met a stuffie that he didn’t think needed to be rescued and cared for,” said his aunt, Swan Sheridan, who described him as “a little ball of energy from the moment he was born.”
Trump says the shooting could have been much worse
President Donald Trump on Friday praised the actions of a “great hero” who he said “took care of business.”
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding the tragedy likely would have been much worse.
At a news conference hours after Thursday’s attack, Gov. Tina Kotek — without naming Giamanco — said he had followed the gunman into the school and helped end the rampage as police began arriving.
“Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” said Kotek.
Memorials with flowers, balloons and stuffed animals popped up around the school, which sits in a densely packed neighborhood filled with newly built homes.
Brooke Olsen, whose daughter is a kindergartner at Silver Rail, said she was amazed that someone pursued the shooter.
“I think it’s miraculous that someone was there before law enforcement even arrived to stop further tragedy from happening,” Olsen said Friday, weeping at times. “I’m feeling very grateful.”
The attacker’s mom bought the gun he used
The 16-year-old suspect, identified only as a Bend resident, was found dead in the school minutes after the first calls for help, Police Chief Mike Krantz said. He shot through locked doors to get inside, police said.
The children who were killed were ages 5, 8 and 11, Krantz said. Authorities didn’t give details about the teacher who was killed. Another 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher were wounded and were taken to a hospital in critical condition, he said Thursday.
The wounded teacher was identified by family as Becky Drury. Her mother-in-law, Yvonne Drury, said on Facebook that she had injuries to her left arm and right hand and was recovering from surgery.
The attacker used a pump-action shotgun bought by his mother, according to a law enforcement official briefed on the shooting. The official spoke to The Associated Press on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to publicly discuss the investigation.
Under Oregon law, a minor may possess a shotgun if provided by a parent or by someone else with the parent’s consent.
Police said they didn’t know if the shooter knew anyone at the school or if he had attended it.
Police respond within minutes
The first 911 call came early in the afternoon from someone outside the school who reported being shot at by someone with a long gun, the police chief said. More 911 calls came from inside the school, police spokesperson Sheila Miller said.
The attacker was shot and went down inside the school shortly after officers arrived, she said.
The school has students in kindergarten through fifth grade, with about 450 enrolled last year, according to the Oregon Department of Education.
Classes and all other activities were canceled Friday for schools across Bend, a tourism and outdoor recreation hub that has ballooned in population and sits about 125 miles (200 kilometers) southeast of Portland.
The shooting was the 28th mass killing in the U.S. this year, according to a database maintained by The Associated Press and USA Today in partnership with Northeastern University.

Bend, Oregon - Kristen Vanetsky and her family moved to Bend, Oregon, after a shooting in their New Mexico neighborhood, choosing Silver Rail Elementary for her grandson because they considered it safer.
But their world was shattered this week when a 16-year-old entered the school and opened fire, shooting dead three children and a teacher, and leaving another child and educator critically wounded.
An armed bystander who pursued the gunman into the school shot and killed him.
The tragic events, Vanetsky told AFP Friday morning outside the school, are "unthinkable."
The 52-year-old, whose 10-year-old grandson attends the school, said the mass shooting "just took away all the innocence" of the school's children, disrupting their sense of safety.
She said she went to the school "trying to make sense of what's going on."
"Who would do this to little kids?"
Thursday's massacre in Bend – a city of about 100,000 people in central Oregon – is the latest of 371 mass shootings that have occurred in the US just this year, according to the tracker Gun Violence Archive.
It "just doesn't stop," Vanetsky said.
She said she is grateful for the actions of the man who fired back against the shooter, but notes the scenario's inherent contradictions, which underscore the ongoing debate over gun control in the US.
"It's very weird, to have a gun solve the problem of a gun," she said. "I can't wrap my mind around it."
"The whole thing could've been a lot worse had somebody not stepped in and shot the shooter," she continued. But now, "the shooter has to live the rest of his life knowing that he shot a 16-year-old to keep other babies from being shot."
"It doesn't make sense," she said tearfully.
"We look out for each other"
Bend, a popular destination for its natural beauty and outdoor recreation scene, "is devastated," Vanetsky said.
"We're a close town of people, and we look out for each other."
And yet, the perpetrator of Thursday's attack was a resident of the city itself.
Authorities have not yet offered details regarding motive or any connection to the school. They did specify that a long gun was used, and media reports indicate the shooter's mother had purchased the weapon.
"I don't understand why a mom would buy a teenage boy a weapon like that," said Vanetsky.

People held candles, sang hymns and prayed as the city began confronting the loss. A teacher from nearby Redmond who attended the vigil wrote “Please protect our children” in sidewalk chalk at the park.

Other Democrats across the U.S., including Senator Jeff Merkley, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and Sentor Cory Booker, also issued statements expressing condolences and calling for greater efforts to prevent gun violence.
The investigation is ongoing as police work to establish a motive and the details surrounding the shooting.

BEND, Oregon >> A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult threw her cellphone at the shooter, tackled him and fought him in an act that saved lives, police said today.
A day into their investigation of the latest U.S. school shooting, authorities released new details of the scene inside a special needs classroom of Silver Rail Elementary School where three school children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, but told a press conference she threw her cell phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.
“She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Krantz said.
As the two wrestled, a parent entered the classroom and opened fire on the gunman, killing him.

He said that the bystander’s actions “undoubtedly saved people,” and “the teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that’s true heroism.”

Oregon elementary school shooter targeted special needs classroom: Police
sources.text:
BEND, Ore. (CN) — Police confirmed on Friday that the 16-year-old suspected shooter who killed four at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school on Thursday targeted a special needs classroom and was a former special needs student at the school himself.
The suspect, whom police identified as Griffin J. John II, killed three children and one adult teacher before being taken down by a bystander.
Bend Police said John, armed with a shotgun, fired at a red pickup truck outside Silver Rail Elementary School before firing multiple rounds into the glass panes of the locked doors to gain entry into the building. Once inside, he fired as many as 15 rounds in a special needs classroom, using three types of ammunition in total.
A 36-year-old man, who police said happened to be passing by the school when he saw John force entry, used a .40 caliber pistol to strike John multiple times, killing him before law enforcement officers arrived on scene.
“I don’t think you can underestimate or underappreciate that courage when someone is willing to risk their own life for others; we recognize that,” Bend Police Department Chief Mike Krantz said at a media briefing on Friday, noting the man who stopped the shooter asked that his name not be publicly released at the briefing. “And the quick thinking to observe, to then park and follow someone into a school is incredible and undoubtedly saved lives.”
Police said a teacher had also intervened to subdue the suspect before the bystander arrived. The teacher threw her cellphone at John, then tackled him and tried to wrestle the firearm away from him.
“She was uninjured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Krantz said, calling the teacher’s actions heroic.
Two of the victims were publicly identified on Friday: 5-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old Megan Lambert. The other victims include an 8-year-old and an 11-year-old.
Two more were injured in the shooting and are still being treated for their injuries: a 7-year-old child and a 54-year-old teacher.
Lambert’s family described her as a passionate teacher and coach.
“To tell you about who Megan was would take 25 years,” Lambert’s family said in a written statement, read aloud at a press conference on Friday. “She was funny, opinionated and she lit up a room.”
Police said that while John had been a former student at the elementary school, he was not currently enrolled in any schools in the district. Authorities did not reveal any possible motive behind the attack.
“Everyone wants to know why, including us,” Krantz said. “That’s part of the current, very active, open investigation we’re working on … we may never get the full answer, but we want it.”
Police are still investigating how John got possession of the shotgun used in the attack.
The fatal shooting on Thursday unfolded quickly. Area dispatchers first received a call at 12:59 p.m. Thursday from the driver of a red pickup truck parked outside the elementary school who reported that someone was shooting at them. Police put the school into lockdown and arrived on the scene three minutes later, finding the suspect already dead.
Bend-La Pine Schools Superintendent Steven Cook said the tragedy has shaken the Silver Rail Elementary School community.
“This has been a terrifying and traumatic experience that will affect us all profoundly for years to come,” Cook said. “Today and the days ahead, we are focused primarily on crisis response and support to everyone in our community and to anyone who’s seeking help.”
Emergency crisis counselors supported over 200 people in Bend over the last 24 hours, and Holly Harris, director of Deschutes County Health Services, said free counseling support will be ongoing as those impacted by the shooting process the event.
“Our community has responded with extraordinary compassion,” Harris said. “In the days ahead, we will continue to stand with one another, care for one another and help carry one another through this unimaginable loss.”

sources.text:
BEND, Oct 16 — A teenager shot and killed three children and a teacher yesterday at an elementary school in the US state of Oregon, police said, adding the assailant was later killed by an armed bystander who pursued him into the building.
Officers rushed to Silver Rail Elementary in Bend, a city of about 100,000 in the nation’s northwest, after reports of a shooter on campus yesterday afternoon.
The three children who died on the scene were aged five, eight and 11, said Bend police chief Mike Krantz. Another child and a teacher were being treated for critical injuries after the shooting.
The United States, where firearms are readily available, has a long and painful history of gun violence, with thousands of people killed every year. It has the highest rate of gun-related deaths among all developed nations.
People gathered in the city’s Drake Park yesterday evening for a candelight vigil remembering the victims.
“I’m in total complete shock, and scared and sad,” said Betsy, who did not give her last name. She spent around 10 minutes contemplating a circle of candles and flowers.
“It’s awful, but it also has brought people together,” she told AFP.
Krantz, the police chief, told journalists that the department first learned of an active shooter after a call from a person who reported being shot at multiple times by a person carrying a long gun.
Dozens of emergency calls then reported that a shooter had entered the school and all law enforcement in the area were called to the scene, the chief added.
Officers arrived at 1:02 pm local time (2002 GMT) within minutes of the calls, he said.
“Moments later, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot by a community member who had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz said.
“Our officers entered the building and confirmed the suspect was dead.”
One seven-year-old and one 54-year-old teacher with critical injuries were transported to a local hospital, he said.
The police chief said the investigation was in its early stages, but told the press conference it appeared “the shooter had forced their way into the school by shooting at locked doors.”
He added that the 16-year-old shooter was a Bend resident.
Unthinkable tragedy
Between 400 and 450 children attend Silver Rail Elementary, where more than 40 staff work, according to a police spokesperson.
After a lockdown, Bend-La Pine School District said law enforcement was escorting students in buses to a separate location, where families could reunite with their children.
The district’s superintendent, Steve Cook, tearfully called the day’s events “an unthinkable tragedy.”
“We are heartbroken. We are horrified. This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places, and pray that it never happens here,” he told reporters.
Parents were anxiously waiting at the site near a church, where Drew Sharp, the father of a fifth grader, the highest grade in the school, told CBS News: “I have faith that he’s okay and that he’ll be alright.”
Children were disembarking from the bus youngest to oldest “which makes sense,” Sharp said, but “it’s just more time waiting.”
Friday classes at schools across the district along with activities and athletic events were canceled, Bend-La Pine said in a statement.
The elementary school is approximately 170 miles (270 kilometers) southeast of the city Portland. It serves primary-age students in kindergarten through fifth grade.
Cannot keep accepting this
The deadliest school shooting in US history took place at Virginia Tech on April 16, 2007, when South Korean student Seung-Hui Cho killed 32 people and wounded 17 others before taking his own life.
There have been more than 360 mass shootings in the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive, which defines a mass shooting as four or more people shot.
“Our hearts are with the terrified children and the families anxiously waiting to hear that their loved ones are safe,” GIFFORDS, a gun safety organization, said on X.
“We cannot keep accepting this as a fact of life.”
Thursday’s shooting was followed by a painfully familiar chorus of calls for action on gun control, pleas that have resulted in little meaningful change.
In the face of decades of massacres, the powerful US pro-gun lobby has given millions of dollars to primarily conservative politicians in a successful bid to keep gun laws loose.
“They’re killing our babies. Shredding our kids with lead. Forcing us to live in fear,” said Janelle Bynum, an Oregon congresswoman, in a statement.
“This continues to happen,” she said later, speaking on CNN. “And it seems as if the adults don’t care.” — AFP

Former mayor of Bend, Oregon, on the deadly shooting at an elementary school
NPR's Steve Inskeep speaks to Jeff Eager, former mayor of Bend, Oregon, about the elementary school shooting in his neighborhood.
STEVE INSKEEP, HOST:
Let's hear now from a member of the community, Jeff Eager, who is the former mayor of Bend, Oregon, and lives a few blocks from the elementary school. Mr. Eager, thanks for joining us.
JEFF EAGER: Thanks for having me, Steve.
INSKEEP: And I'm sorry this would happen to your community or any community. What was your experience yesterday?
EAGER: Well, my experience was I was working here in my home office. Didn't hear anything happen out there. Got a phone call about half an hour after the event and walked over there. The biggest thing that struck me was just how quiet everything was. I mean, there were hundreds of parents, dozens of law enforcement officers, and it was nearly silent. I guess, I'd never thought about what the aftermath of a school shooting would be like, but I learned that it's quiet.
INSKEEP: I'm thinking about what that silence means. I suppose one thing it means is that after so many shootings, everybody there knew what this was.
EAGER: Yes. I think so.
INSKEEP: We heard from Arezou that this was a school and a school district that seemed to have made preparations for this kind of event. There was a lockdown within a couple of minutes of a 911 call. Officers arrived very quickly. How well prepared was this community for such an occasion?
EAGER: I think pretty well prepared, as sad as that is to say. Like you said, the response time was very fast. You know, the school district has invested significant sums in security in recent years. This was about a 10-year-old school, so relatively new, presumably had decent security in it. Obviously, whatever was there didn't work.
INSKEEP: How do you think about the days ahead?
EAGER: I think there's going to be a lot of sadness. I think that the Bend community is - it's a strong one. It will excel as it helps people through this process. It's a good place, and we know how to take care of each other. And that's what I expect to see.

1. A 16-year-old killed three children and a teacher at a Bend, Oregon, elementary school Oct. 15.
2. A father of two students followed him inside and shot him dead, police and his brother said.
3. A 7-year-old and a second teacher were hospitalized in critical condition.
A 16-year-old gunman killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Oct. 15 before a man who saw him enter the building followed him inside and shot him dead, police said. A second teacher, 54, and a 7-year-old were in critical condition at St. Charles Medical Center in Bend.
The man who stopped the shooting has been identified as Kaylub Giamanco, a 36-year-old carpenter whose two daughters attend the school, his brother Kyle Giamanco told NBC News.
Giamanco was on his way back from a lunch break when he spotted the gunman entering the school, and because he holds a concealed-carry permit he “decided to go in after” him, his brother said. Kyle Giamanco added that his brother does not want to speak publicly yet because he feels guilt over the children he could not save, and the family said in a statement Oct. 16 that he is “not seeking recognition.”
How the Attack Unfolded
The first 911 call came at 12:59 p.m. from a driver who said someone with a long gun had shot at him several times, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz told reporters that evening. Dispatchers then took dozens of calls reporting a shooter inside the school, which serves kindergarten through fifth grade and has more than 400 students. The teen got into the building by shooting through locked doors, police said.
Officers reached the school at 1:02 p.m., within three minutes of the first call, and learned that a community member had already shot the suspect. The man “had seen the suspect enter the school and pursued him into the school and engaged him,” Krantz said.
Officers confirmed the teen was dead, treated the wounded and evacuated the school room by room, busing children to a reunification site at a nearby church. Several parents said the shooting took place in a special education classroom, which police have not confirmed.
The family of the 5-year-old identified him as Rhoam Summer. His father, Kelik Summer, wrote on Facebook that Oct. 15 was “the worst day of my life.” The other victims have not been named, and police said all of their families have been notified.
Police have not released the suspect’s name or a motive, and have not said whether he had ties to the school. He used a pump-action shotgun his mother bought around his August birthday, and she has cooperated with investigators, officials told NBC News. Oregon bars anyone under 18 from buying a rifle or shotgun but allows minors to possess one with a parent’s consent. The FBI and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are assisting.
Gov. Tina Kotek thanked the community member who “heroically intervened to stop further loss of life” and ordered flags at state buildings lowered to half-staff. President Donald Trump praised Giamanco Oct. 16, telling reporters that “we had a great hero that went in and did the business.”
What’s Next: Bend-La Pine Schools canceled classes and activities, and police said officers will remain at the school in large numbers for several days. “This is going to be a long investigation,” Krantz said.

sources.news_title: Oregon teacher fought school attacker before armed dad shot suspect 'multiple times'
sources.text:
Some readers may find this article distressing.
An Oregon teacher threw her mobile phone before she tackled and tried to wrestle away a shotgun from the arms of a teen suspect who opened fire on a special educational needs class.
As she tussled with him on the floor of the class – where three children and a teacher were killed – a bystander armed with a pistol ran inside and killed the teen.
The bystander, a father of two girls at the school, had been driving past Silver Rail Elementary in Bend on Thursday lunchtime when he saw the suspect firing in the car park, then shooting through a window to enter.
Police said the 16-year-old suspect used to be a student at the school.
Police say the suspect was armed with about 44 more rounds of shotgun ammunition when he was stopped. He fired as many as 15 rounds in the class.
“To the people who showed courage in the face of such violence, and intervened to prevent this tragedy from being any worse, we owe you a debt of gratitude,” Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said on Friday.
Police offered more information on the attack at a news conference on Friday, where they identified two of the four victims. They include five-year-old Rhoam Summer and 25-year-old teacher Meghan Lambert.
The families of the two other students who were killed, an eight-year-old and 11-year-old, did not wish to have them publicly identified yet, police said.
Two others were injured in the attack. Another teacher, a 54-year-old, was still being treated at hospital, and a seven-year-old student, who was in serious but stable condition.
Krantz said the heroic actions of both the teacher and the father who ran inside the school saved lives.
He said the teacher who wrestled with the gunman was not hurt but “almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed”.
He identified the suspect as 16-year-old Griffin J John II, who previously attended the school and was a special educational needs student there.
A search warrant has been executed at the suspect’s home and a search is ongoing, the police chief said.
Police believe the suspect travelled to the elementary school on foot, but they are still investigating his exact movements and how he acquired the gun. A motive is also not clear.
Officials did not confirm the name of the father who intervened and fatally shot the suspect.
But Kaylub Giamanco’s family has identified him to US media as the person who sprang into action.
The 36-year-old carpenter had just finished lunch and was on his way home when he passed the school, his brother told NBC News. He saw the suspect open fire on a vehicle outside the school then shoot through a window and go inside.
Police said he had a legally concealed .40 calibre in his vehicle and his brother said he grabbed the pistol “and decided to go in after” the suspect. Police say he fired at the suspect “multiple times”, killing him.
Giamanco’s mother, Kenda Freeman, who lives in Sacramento, California, told a local CBS station her son had called her moments after the shooting, and he was “traumatised”.
“He said a man went into my daughter’s school,” Freeman said, pausing as she started to tear up. “And, um, shot kids. And he said, and I looked at him point blank, and I shot and killed him, mom.”
She added: “I told him he saved a lot of lives, and he said, mom, I couldn’t save them all.”
US President Donald Trump praised the bystander on Friday, calling him a “great hero”.
Addressing reporters at the White House before departing for Georgia, Trump said the situation could have been “much worse” with no intervention.
“It’s a terrible thing, but thank goodness for a man that had a gun and knew how to use it,” he said.
Without naming the bystander, Oregon Governor Tina Kotek acknowledged the man’s heroic actions stopping further loss of life, but noted they “carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well”.
Kayla Epstein contributed to this report.

sources.news_title: Bend Police Identify 16-Year-Old Gunman, Reveal New Details of Deadly Attack
sources.text:
BEND, Ore. (Oct. 16, 2026) — Bend police released new details Friday about the deadly shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School, identifying the 16-year-old suspect and describing how a teacher and a parent of students at the school intervened during an attack that killed three children and a teacher Thursday afternoon.
The shooting occurred shortly before 1 p.m. Oct. 15 at Silver Rail Elementary School, located at 61530 SE Stone Creek Lane in Bend.
Five people died at the scene, including the suspected shooter. The victims included three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a 25-year-old teacher. Two others, a 7-year-old girl and a 54-year-old teacher, were critically injured.
During a Friday news conference, Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz acknowledged the devastating impact of the shooting and thanked community members who gathered for a vigil Thursday evening.
“Yesterday was a terrible day for our community, and I appreciate the thousands of people who showed up at last night’s vigil at Drake Park because you care about each other, and that mattered,” Krantz said. “That is what community looks like.”
Police Detail Suspect’s Movements Before Shooting
Investigators identified the suspected shooter as 16-year-old Griffin J. John II, a former student at Silver Rail Elementary School who was not currently enrolled in Bend-La Pine Schools.
Police believe John traveled to the school on foot, although investigators are still working to determine his exact route.
According to police, the incident began at approximately 12:58 p.m. Thursday as two vehicles traveled westbound on Brentwood Avenue near the school.
Investigators said John approached the school’s fenced rear perimeter from an undeveloped area near Nina Avenue. He allegedly crossed the street, threw a shotgun over the fence and climbed onto school property.
The driver of a red Toyota pickup witnessed the incident and verbally confronted the suspect.
Police said the suspect responded by firing at the pickup, striking it at least three times.
The driver continued down the street and placed the initial 911 call at 12:59 p.m., reporting that someone armed with a long gun had fired multiple shots at his vehicle.
A second driver, a 36-year-old man whose children attend Silver Rail Elementary, also witnessed the confrontation and drove into the school’s parking lot.
Suspect Forced Entry Into Classroom
Investigators said the suspect walked westbound along the south side of the school before approaching a set of exterior double doors.
He fired multiple rounds into the glass panes of the doors to gain entry.
Once inside, the suspect immediately entered a classroom to the left of the entrance and opened fire.
Police estimate the suspect fired as many as 15 rounds during the incident, although the exact number discharged inside the classroom remains under investigation.
All six shooting victims were inside that classroom.
Investigators determined that three types of 12-gauge ammunition were used during the attack: birdshot, buckshot and slugs.
Teacher and Parent Intervened During Attack
Police credited two individuals with taking extraordinary action to confront the shooter.
According to investigators, a teacher inside the classroom threw her cellphone at the suspect before physically tackling him and attempting to wrestle the shotgun away.
The teacher was not injured during the confrontation.
Meanwhile, the 36-year-old father who had witnessed the initial shooting outside the school retrieved a legally secured .40-caliber pistol from his vehicle.
He entered the building through the doors the suspect had forced open.
Inside, the man witnessed the teacher physically struggling with the suspect and fired his handgun, striking the 16-year-old multiple times.
The suspect died at the scene.
Police said the actions of the teacher and the parent were instrumental in confronting the gunman during the attack.
Victims Identified, Conditions Updated
Police confirmed Friday that one of the children killed was 5-year-old Rhoam Summer. His identity was released at the request of his family.
The families of the other two children killed, ages 8 and 11, have requested that their identities not be publicly released.
The teacher who died was identified as 25-year-old Megan Lambert of Bend.
Investigators said two of the children and Lambert were already deceased when responding officers arrived. Officers and emergency medical personnel attempted lifesaving measures on another boy at the scene, but he did not survive.
Two additional victims remain hospitalized.
A 7-year-old girl who received lifesaving treatment at the school was transported for medical care and is now hospitalized at Oregon Health & Science University in Portland. Police said she remains in serious but stable condition.
The injured teacher, identified with her family’s permission as 54-year-old Becky Drury of Bend, remains hospitalized at St. Charles Bend.
Police said Drury sustained serious injuries that are not considered life-threatening.
Officers Arrived Within Minutes
Bend police provided an updated timeline of the emergency response.
The initial 911 call was received by Deschutes County Dispatch at 12:59 p.m. Thursday.
Dispatchers subsequently received dozens of emergency calls reporting an armed individual inside Silver Rail Elementary School.
At 1 p.m., dispatch issued an emergency alert to law enforcement personnel.
Responding officers directed the school to initiate lockdown procedures at 1:01 p.m.
The first officers arrived at 1:02 p.m., approximately three minutes after the initial emergency call.
Moments later, an officer reported that the suspect had been shot multiple times by a community member.
Students and staff were subsequently transported aboard Bend-La Pine Schools buses to Journey Church, where they were reunited with parents and guardians.
Shotgun and Additional Ammunition Recovered
Officers responding to the shooting recovered a Maverick 88 pump-action 12-gauge shotgun near the deceased suspect.
Investigators also located a backpack containing additional ammunition.
Police said approximately 44 rounds of 12-gauge ammunition remained on the suspect or inside the backpack.
Authorities have not determined how the 16-year-old obtained the shotgun or ammunition.
Those questions remain part of the active criminal investigation.
Investigation Involves Approximately 150 Personnel
Bend police have activated the Tri-County Major Incident Team to assist with the investigation.
Approximately 150 law enforcement officers and emergency response personnel have participated in the response and subsequent investigation.
Agencies involved include the Deschutes County Sheriff’s Office, Redmond Police Department, Oregon State Police, FBI and Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives.
Investigators have completed a digital scan of the school and collected physical evidence from the scene.
Authorities also executed a search warrant at the suspect’s residence.
Interviews with witnesses and others connected to the incident remain ongoing.
Police conducted a second walkthrough of the school Friday morning and said investigators do not anticipate releasing the scene until Tuesday, Oct. 20, at the earliest.
The extended timeline is intended to ensure investigators have sufficient time to document the scene and collect all available evidence.
The FBI’s Victim Services Division will coordinate with Bend-La Pine Schools to assist students, families and staff who need to retrieve belongings from unaffected areas of the building.
Community Mourns as Investigation Continues
The shooting has left the Bend community mourning the deaths of three young children and an elementary school teacher while two additional victims continue recovering from their injuries.
Thousands of residents gathered at Drake Park on Thursday evening to honor those killed and support the families affected by the tragedy.
Authorities continue working to establish the circumstances leading up to the shooting, including how the suspect acquired the firearm and ammunition and what prompted the attack.
Police have not released information establishing a motive.
The investigation remains active, and additional information is expected as investigators continue examining evidence and interviewing witnesses.

sources.news_title: Shooter in fatal Bend, Oregon, school shooting was former student there
sources.text:
The 16-year-old who barged into an elementary school in Bend, Oregon, and unleashed a barrage of gunfire that killed a teacher and three children was a former student at Silver Rail elementary, officials confirmed in a Friday press conference.
The heavily armed gunman, identified as Griffin J John II, climbed over a fence and onto the school’s property before shooting through a set of locked doors to enter the building.
The shooter, a former special needs learner, beelined toward a special education classroom left of the entrance doors, firing as many as 15 rounds.
All of the victims from Thursday’s shooting were in that room: five-year-old Rhoam Summer, two other students, ages eight and 11, whom authorities have not identified, and 25-year-old teacher Megan Lambert.
Lambert, a central Oregon native regarded Silver Rail as a “dream job”, her family said in a statement read by police. “She always fought for the underdog and those with special needs.”
The shooting also left a seven-year-old still in serious condition, police said, and 54-year-old educator Becky Drury with serious, but non-life-threatening injuries.
A 36-year-old Silver Rail parent, identified by relatives as Kaylub Giamanco , heard the gunshots as he was driving by and entered the school.
He saw an educator in a scuffle with the gunman, at which point he intervened, shooting and killing the teen.
Police say the teacher threw her phone at the shooter before tackling him, as she fought to disarm him.
“She almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Bend police chief Mike Krantz said.
Authorities recovered 44 more rounds of ammunition in the shooter’s backpack.
Police have not offered a motive, citing the continuing investigation.
Candlelight vigils and memorials have sprung up around Bend, as the city has been thrust into a gruesome, but tragically familiar American story.
Outside the school on Friday, a steady stream of people arrived to deliver flowers in front of the campus.
They left dozens of bouquets, teddy bears, Minnie Mouse stuffed animals and a pumpkin. Most people stopped by for just a moment to pay their respects. Some sat, and parents held their children and cried together.
It was eerily quiet at a time when the campus would normally be teeming with activity, said Joe Camarlinghi, father of a third grader at the school.
Fabiola Caseres, who runs a local preschool and came by to deliver flowers, said the sadness was palpable all around the close-knit city.
“It just feels so heavy,” she said. “Everybody is looking like deer in the headlights. It’s so sad, and you can’t stop thinking about the kids. They’re supposed to come home.”
Thursday’s events mark the most deadly school shooting since the September 2024 mass killing at Apalachee high school in Georgia, where a 14-year-old shooter killed two teachers and two students.
Although a motive in this school shooting remains unclear, the age of the shooter points to a troubling pattern.
Some of the most recent high-profile shootings on and off school campuses have been carried out by teenagers and young adults, many of whom are a part of nihilistic online communities where posters praise, and seek to emulate, prior shooters like those who carried out attacks at Columbine high school, in Christchurch in New Zealand and at Virginia Tech.
In May, two teenagers who met and were radicalized online shot and killed three people at a mosque in San Diego before shooting themselves. In their manifesto, they explicitly named the Apalachee high school shooters as their inspiration.
The city of Bend, home to about 100,000 residents, held a candlelit vigil on Thursday night. Hundreds of people gathered in Bend’s Drake Park as the sun set. Oregon governor Tina Kotek and Bend mayor Melanie Kebler attended the vigil.
“There is power and love in this park tonight,” Kotek said. “On behalf of everyone who lives in Oregon, I am so sorry for what you are experiencing today. No parent, no family, no community should have to have this kind of day.”
All schools in Bend and La Pine, a neighboring city, were closed on Friday.

sources.news_title: Teacher Fights Oregon School Shooter, Credited With Helping Prevent Further Bloodshed
sources.text:
- Shooter killed 3 schoolchildren ages 5, 8 and 11 plus a teacher.
- Another student and teacher were also wounded.
- Shooter of suspect also hailed as hero.
A teacher in the Oregon classroom where a shooter killed three children and an adult threw her cellphone at the shooter, tackled him and fought him in an act that saved lives, police said on Friday.
A day into their investigation of the latest US school shooting, authorities released new details of the scene inside a special needs classroom of Silver Rail Elementary School where three school children aged 5, 8 and 11 and a teacher were killed by a 16-year-old former student.
Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz did not identify the teacher who fought the assailant, but told a press conference she threw her cell phone at the suspect, tackled him and fought to take his shotgun from him.
“She was not injured in that incident, but she almost certainly helped prevent more bloodshed,” Krantz said.
As the two wrestled, a parent entered the classroom and opened fire on the gunman, killing him.
Officials said the parent had followed the shooter into the school upon witnessing him firing a shotgun from just outside campus. By the time police arrived within three minutes of receiving their first call, the shooter was dead, police said.
In the meantime, the 16-year-old assailant, who had shot through locked glass doors to enter campus, had killed four people and wounded two others.
Krantz, speaking to the heroism shown by the teacher who threw herself onto the suspect and the parent who shot him, said, “I don’t think we can underestimate or underappreciate that courage. When someone is willing to risk their own life for others, we recognise that.”
He said that the bystander’s actions “undoubtedly saved people,” and “the teacher who was willing to stand and fight for her children, that’s true heroism.”
Krantz identified the shooter as Griffin J. John II, who was armed with a 12-gauge shotgun. He fired about 15 rounds in the classroom and had another 44 rounds on him.
The parent who killed the shooter was identified as Kaylub Giamanco, his mother told the New York Times.
She identified him as the father of two girls who attend the school, according to video posted by the New York Times of Freeman reading a brief statement.

A teacher who was in a classroom on campus during the entire ordeal, Kathy Sheil Smith, spoke with CNN affiliate KPTV on Thursday night, saying of the students: “They were so afraid. The looks on their faces was really hard to see.”
Speaking to what occurred on the ground, she saw the shooter enter the school from her classroom window. After alerting the main office, she moved her students to a corner of the classroom to shelter in place. “Some kids were praying; some kids were consoling other kids,” Smith said.
As shots were heard across the school, she said some teachers imagined they wouldn’t make it out alive.
“I’m sure that every teacher at the school thought, ‘Today is the day that I am going to die,’” she said through tears.
The tragedy has prompted an outpouring of pastoral care and community support across the state, with hundreds attending a candelight vigil Thursday night.

Local officials and state leaders emphasized the need for communal healing, counseling, and mutual support in the days ahead.

John J Griffin, 16, the teenager accused of killing three children and a teacher at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, had previously attended the school, according to emerging details about the attack.
The shooting happened on Thursday, when Griffin allegedly entered the school at approximately 12.59pm carrying a pump-action long gun. Police said the firearm had been purchased by his mother.
The attack left four people dead and two others critically injured. Authorities have not established a motive for the shooting.
Gunman Allegedly Fired at Vehicle Before Entering School
Investigators said the attack began in the school car park, where the suspect allegedly opened fire on a red Toyota Tacoma pickup truck.
Images shared online showed multiple bullet holes in the vehicle, along with a shattered rear passenger-side window.
The suspect allegedly threw the firearm over the school fence before climbing over it himself and entering the premises. The driver of the truck contacted Deschutes County dispatchers shortly before 1pm.
Silver Rail Elementary School serves approximately 450 children and is located in Bend, around 160 miles southeast of Portland.
Three Children and Teacher Killed in Special Education Area
According to the account of the attack, Griffin allegedly fired at locked doors before reaching the school’s special education area, where three children aged five, eight and 11 were killed alongside a teacher.
The youngest victim was identified as five-year-old Rhoam Summer. His father confirmed his identity on Friday.
A 54-year-old teacher and a seven-year-old child who uses a wheelchair were also taken to hospital in critical condition. The child had been shot in the face.
Authorities have not provided an updated account of the two injured victims’ conditions.
Father of Two Children at School Shot Suspect Dead
The shooting ended when Kalub Giamanco, 36, confronted the teenager inside the school and shot him dead.
Giamanco, whose two children attend Silver Rail Elementary, was reportedly driving home for his lunch break when he heard gunfire. He entered the school and pursued the suspect.
Emergency medical services dispatch audio suggested that the person who shot the gunman may have been a father at the school.
“Looks like the shooter has been neutralized, possibly shot by a father at the school,” a staff member was heard saying in the audio, according to a report by the BBC.
The suspect was killed approximately three minutes before police arrived. Authorities have not publicly confirmed further details about the identity of the person who confronted him.
Fifth-grade teacher Kathy Sheil Smith praised the individual who intervened, saying the person had acted courageously and expressing gratitude that the suspect had been stopped.
Police Search Suspect’s Family Home
Police raided Griffin’s family home on Thursday night and seized computers and other electronic devices as part of their investigation.
His parents were reported to have cooperated with authorities.
Investigators have not disclosed whether Griffin had previously made threats, experienced disciplinary problems or displayed other warning signs. They have also not confirmed whether he possessed additional weapons or whether a note or other digital evidence was recovered.
Authorities have yet to establish why the teenager allegedly carried out the attack or provide a complete account of how he moved through the school.
The police chief warned that the investigation would take time, with officers expected to remain at the scene for several days.
Investigation Continues as Community Mourns Victims
The attack has added to the number of deadly shootings at American schools. According to the K-12 School Shooting Database, 235 shooting incidents were recorded at US schools last year, with at least 140 reported so far this year.
Oregon has introduced several gun safety laws in recent years and was ranked 12th among the 50 states for the strength of its gun laws by Everytown for Gun Safety.

Investigators continue to examine the circumstances surrounding the Silver Rail Elementary School shooting, including the suspect’s background, the weapon used and the events leading up to the attack.

The elementary school, which has more than 400 students and 40 staff members, was placed under lockdown as school busses took students and teachers to a church away from campus to reunify with family members. The school has kindergarten through fifth grade classes, according to The Associated Press.
“This is the kind of thing you hear about in other places and pray that it never happens here,” said Bend-La Pine Schools superintendent Steven Cook. “And it has happened here.”
Cook announced all schools and school events will be canceled Friday. Police will also be present at Silver Rail Elementary School for the next few days.
Community members in Bend, located about 150 miles south of Portland, gathered Thursday evening for a vigil at Drake Park. Crisis counselors will be at Deschutes Central Library on Friday to support those who are grieving.
U.S. Rep. Janelle Bynum, whose congressional district includes Bend, said she would halt campaign activity to focus on supporting the community, The Oregonian reported.
“They’re killing our babies,” Bynum said in a Thursday statement. “Our babies are supposed to do arts and crafts at school, not use their desks as cover from gunfire. They’re supposed to make friends, not mourn them. This is every parent’s worst fear. My heart and my prayers and everything else I got is with the families at Silver Rail Elementary. When will it end?”
Washington lawmakers reacted to the shooting on social media.
“Truly no words for the absolute horror of what unfolded at Silver Rail Elementary today,” wrote U.S. Rep. Suzan DelBene, who represents the 1st Congressional District. “Schools should be safe havens for our children, not places of unthinkable violence.”
Oregon Gov. Tina Kotek said her heart was “absolutely broken” and thanked the civilian who pursued the shooter, The Associated Press reported.
“To the community member who heroically intervened to stop further loss of life: Your actions carry a heavy emotional burden, and I just want you to know that my thoughts are with you as well,” she said.
